task: Write an analytical essay on how the poet presents the relationship between inheritance and loss in the poem 'Inheritance' by Maren Idowu.
text:
In "Inheritance", Maren Idowu presents what we receive from the people who came before us as something both precious and incomplete: a gift that arrives already damaged by absence. Through a speaker who tries to rebuild her grandmother from domestic objects, Idowu suggests that inheritance is less about what is handed down than about what is withheld, and that grieving for something never fully possessed is a distinct and quieter kind of loss.

The poem opens with a metaphor that sets up this paradox: "My grandmother's hands were maps of a country / I was only ever shown the borders of." The creased hands resemble contour lines, a record of an entire life, yet the speaker can read only the edges. The verb "shown" matters, because it makes the grandmother's reticence an act rather than an accident; the speaker was a visitor to this country, never a citizen. The enjambment after "country" lets the reader hold, for a moment, the idea of a whole homeland before the second line narrows it to "borders", and that small delay mirrors the speaker's experience of nearly arriving and being turned back. The word "only" lets a note of resentment slip into a poem that otherwise works hard to sound calm.

The title itself is quietly ironic. "Inheritance" suggests wills, property and legal certainty, yet what the speaker inherits has no market value and cannot be itemised: a language, a name, a way of standing in a kitchen. By borrowing the vocabulary of legal transfer for something so intangible, Idowu hints that the most important things families pass on are exactly the things that cannot be guaranteed to survive the handover.

Idowu develops the idea of withholding through a domestic image: the grandmother "folded the language into drawers, / the way you fold a good tablecloth: / for guests who never came." The simile is deceptively gentle. A good tablecloth is kept for occasions, so the language, presumably the family's mother tongue, is treated as too valuable for everyday use, and so it is never used and never passed on. The tone is wistful rather than angry, and the phrase "for guests who never came" shifts the blame onto circumstance, perhaps migration or the fear of seeming foreign, rather than onto the grandmother herself. This ambiguity is what gives the poem its maturity: the speaker cannot decide whether her grandmother protected the language or buried it. The repeated sounds of "folded" and "fold" also enact the careful, habitual motion of putting something away.

Structure carries the argument as much as imagery does. The poem is in free verse with irregular line lengths, but the stanzas shrink as it goes on, and the final stanza is a couplet: "Now I say her name wrong / and the kitchen forgives me." The narrowing of the stanzas imitates the dwindling of what is remembered. Here the loss is not a dramatic death but a mispronunciation, a failure so ordinary that it could easily go unnoticed. The personification of the kitchen is the poem's most striking choice. The room where the grandmother presumably spent her life is given the power to forgive, which implies that the speaker cannot forgive herself and that the one person who could has gone. There is no rhyme and no consoling flourish, and the plain monosyllables of "forgives me" leave a hush more moving than any lament would be.

It is also significant that the speaker positions herself as an inheritor of silence. The completed past tense of the grandmother's actions, "were" and "folded", is set against the present tense of "Now", in which the speaker is still in the act of losing. This contrast suggests that inheritance is not a single transfer but an ongoing process, in which a culture can be lost a little more each time a name is said wrongly. In this sense Idowu argues that loss is not the opposite of inheritance but part of it: to inherit a heritage is also to inherit the responsibility for its disappearance.

Ultimately, "Inheritance" presents what we are given as a map with only the borders drawn, an invitation to a country we may never fully enter. Idowu's restrained diction, domestic imagery and shrinking structure make the grief feel earned rather than sentimental. The final gentleness, in which a room forgives where people cannot, offers a consolation that does not cancel the loss, and that refusal to console is exactly what makes the poem convincing.

task: Write an analytical essay on how John Steinbeck presents loneliness in Of Mice and Men.
text:
In Of Mice and Men, John Steinbeck presents loneliness as something that follows people through the whole of society in 1930s America, not just a feeling that some characters have. By showing us several lonely characters, and by setting the novella on a ranch full of men who are only temporarily together, Steinbeck suggests that loneliness is a result of the Depression and of the way that society treats the weak. This essay will look at how he does this through George and Lennie, Crooks and Curley's wife.

Firstly, Steinbeck shows loneliness as the normal condition of the ranch worker. Early in the novella George tells Lennie that "guys like us, that work on ranches, are the loneliest guys in the world." The use of the superlative "loneliest" shows how extreme this isolation is, and the phrase "guys like us" makes it a shared problem and not just George's own. George goes on to say that they "got no family" and "don't belong no place". The repetition of negatives shows how little the men have, and Steinbeck makes the dialect sound natural so that the reader feels George is speaking from real experience. Because of this, the friendship between George and Lennie is special and unusual. Lennie says "I got you to look after me, and you got me to look after you", which shows that their friendship is a kind of protection against the loneliness all around them. The balanced structure of the sentence suggests that they are equal, even though Lennie is the one who is dependent, and this makes the reader admire them.

Secondly, Crooks is the character who shows loneliness most clearly. Because he is Black he has to live in a separate room in the barn, and Steinbeck makes the setting reflect his isolation. His room is described as being full of his possessions, like his books and tools, which suggests that he has filled his life with objects because he has no people. When Lennie comes in, Crooks at first tries to send him away but then gives in to the chance to talk, and he says "A guy goes nuts if he ain't got nobody." This is a strong line because it shows that loneliness is not just sad but actually dangerous to a person's mind. The fact that Crooks needs to talk so much, and then talks cruelly to Lennie about George not coming back, shows that his loneliness has made him bitter. Steinbeck may be showing that racism is a cause of this loneliness, which makes the novella a criticism of society as well as a story about individuals.

Curley's wife is another example. She is not given a name, which tells the reader she is seen only as property belonging to her husband, and the men on the ranch avoid her because they are afraid of Curley. She tells Lennie that she "ain't got nobody to talk to", and that she could have been a movie star. Her loneliness is made worse by her dreams being so far from the truth. I think Steinbeck wants us to feel sympathy for her even though she is shown by other men as a troublemaker. In some ways her loneliness is the same as Crooks, because they are both excluded, but the difference is that she tries to get attention through flirting, which makes the men even more distant.

Finally, the ending shows that George's loneliness is the real tragedy. After George shoots Lennie by the river, the way the novella is built in a circle, returning to the pool where it began, makes it feel as if nothing has changed except that George is now truly alone. Slim says "You hadda, George", which is kind, but it cannot take away what has happened. The reader understands that without Lennie, George will become just like the other ranch workers who "come an' go", and the dream of the farm is gone for good.

In conclusion, Steinbeck presents loneliness through many characters, and shows that it is caused by poverty, racism and the position of women in society. By using dialect, repetition and setting, he makes the reader see that the friendship of George and Lennie is rare and valuable, and that its loss at the end is what makes the novella so sad.

task: Write an analytical essay on how William Golding presents the loss of civilisation in Lord of the Flies.
text:
Lord of the Flies is a novel by William Golding about a group of boys who are stranded on an island after a plane crash and what happens to them when there are no adults. In this essay I am going to explain how Golding shows the loss of civilisation in the novel and what he is trying to say about people.

At the start of the novel the boys are quite civilised. Ralph finds the conch shell and he blows it to call the other boys together. This is important because the conch is used to call meetings and the person who holds the conch is allowed to speak. So at the beginning the boys have rules and they vote for Ralph to be chief. Jack is not happy about this because he wanted to be chief, and he says he will be in charge of the choir and they will be hunters. Piggy is also in the story and he has glasses and he is fat and the other boys do not like him but he is very clever. Ralph says they need a fire so a ship can see them and rescue them. They use Piggy's glasses to start the fire. The fire is a symbol of rescue and it also shows that the boys want to be civilised at the start.

After a while, things start to go wrong. The boys do not do their jobs. Jack and the hunters are meant to look after the fire but they go hunting a pig instead, and while they are gone a ship goes past and the fire is out. Ralph is very angry about this and he shouts at Jack, but Jack just does not care because he only wants to hunt. This shows the beginning of the loss of civilisation because the boys are no longer thinking about being rescued, they are only thinking about what they want. Golding is showing that when there is no one to tell people what to do they will do what they want.

Then there is the problem of the beast. The little boys say they have seen a beast and they are scared. The older boys do not know what to do. Then the twins Sam and Eric see the dead parachutist on the mountain and they think it is the beast, so everyone is more scared. Jack uses the fear to get more power. He says that Ralph is a coward and he starts his own tribe and goes to live at Castle Rock. A lot of the boys go with Jack because he gives them meat and he lets them paint their faces. The painting of faces is important because it makes them feel like they are someone else so they do not feel ashamed. This shows that they are becoming savages. The boys then chant "Kill the beast! Cut his throat! Spill his blood!" which shows how violent they have become.

The worst part is when Simon is killed. Simon goes to tell everyone that the beast is just a dead man, but the boys are in a dance and in the dark they think he is the beast and they kill him. This is very sad because Simon was a good character and he was the only one who really understood the island. After this Piggy is killed as well when Roger pushes a big rock down on him and the conch is smashed. When the conch breaks, it shows that there are no more rules at all and that civilisation has gone completely. Ralph is then hunted by Jack's tribe, who set the island on fire to smoke him out. Ralph runs along the beach until he gets to a naval officer, who is surprised because he thinks they were just playing a game. Ralph cries because he knows what has happened to them, and he cries for Piggy and for the end of innocence.

Golding was writing after the Second World War and he had seen how terrible people can be, so I think this is why he wrote the novel. He wants to show that people are not always good and that without rules they will turn into savages. The island is a bit like the world, and the adult at the end is a bit like how the adults in the war were also fighting but with bigger guns, so that the naval officer is not so different to the boys. This makes the ending quite clever because the officer is also a hunter in a way.

To conclude, Golding shows the loss of civilisation in lots of ways. The conch, the fire, the painting of faces and the killings all show how the boys changed from being civilised to being savages. It is a very powerful novel and it is still important today because it makes us think about how people behave when no one is in charge. In my opinion it is a really good book and it shows the loss of civilisation very well.

task: Write an analytical essay on how J.B. Priestley presents responsibility in An Inspector Calls.
text:
An Inspector Calls is a play by JB Priestley. It is about a family called the Birlings who are having a dinner party and then an Inspector comes and he asks them questions about a girl who died. The girl was called Eva Smith. The inspector shows that every one of them did something bad to her. This is how Priestley shows responsibility in the play.

First Mr Birling was the one who sacked her from his factory because she asked for more money. He thinks he did nothing wrong and he is rude. Then Sheila got her sacked from a shop because she was jealous and she was sorry about it afterwards. Then Gerald had an affair with her and he was in a lot of the play. Then Mrs Birling would not help her when she asked for money from the charity and she was very mean to her and said that it was the fathers fault. Then it turns out that Eric was the father of the baby and he took money from his dad's work. So they all did something.

The Inspector is very important in the play because he makes them all say what they did. He says we are all members of one body. At the end the Inspector leaves and then Mr Birling finds out that he was not a real inspector and he thinks that it is all ok. But then the phone rings and it says a girl has died and a real inspector is coming. This is a good ending because you want to know what will happen next.

Priestley wants us to think that we should all take responsibility and not just think about ourselves. Mr Birling does not learn but Sheila and Eric do. I think this shows that the older people do not change and the younger people do. The play is good because it makes you think about being responsible. In conclusion Priestley shows responsibility by showing the Birlings all being part of her death and I think it is a good play.

task: Creative writing: write a short story or descriptive piece that begins with the line 'The last bus had already left.'
text:
The last bus had already left. I knew it from the way the shelter hummed, empty, with its one flickering strip light buzzing against the dark like a trapped insect. On the timetable under the cracked perspex somebody had scratched a line through 11:48 and written, in biro, as if in apology, gone.

I sat down anyway. My phone was at four per cent and my mother's name was on the screen, the way it had been for three hours, a small green circle I kept not pressing. I turned the phone face down on my knee and listened to the town. Somewhere a shutter rattled. A fox crossed the road without looking either way, which is more than I had managed all evening.

I should say what I had done, because pretending otherwise would be a lie of its own. I had told my mother I was at Priya's revising. Priya, who had covered for me twice before, had covered for me a third time, and the lie had held until about nine, when the party in the flat above the chip shop got loud enough that someone filmed it and someone else posted it, and my face, flushed and laughing in the background, had travelled through four group chats and arrived, by ten, in my aunt's pocket. By ten past, my mother knew. That was the green circle. She had not shouted. She had sent a single message that read, Come home when you are ready. I would have preferred the shouting.

The cold came up through the bench into my spine. A taxi slid past, its sign lit like a held breath, and I did not wave it down, because I had eleven pounds and the fare would have taken all of it, and because some stubborn part of me wanted the walk to be hard. If I got home too easily, it would not count as anything.

So I walked. The road out of town bends along the canal and the lamps there are spaced too far apart, so that you move from one pool of orange light into a long stretch of nothing and out again. In the dark stretches I could hear my own shoes, and under them the thin, steady sound of the water that did not care about me at all. I found it strangely comforting. Everything I had been rehearsing for three hours, the speech about being sixteen, about trust, about how she never let me do anything, seemed to loosen and drift away from me and sink in the canal like a coin.

What I kept seeing was her hands. When I was small, she used to wait up at the kitchen table, not doing anything, just holding a mug she never drank from, so that I would see the light under the door and know I had been expected. I had always thought of it as surveillance. Walking beside the black water, I started to wonder whether it had ever been anything other than waiting.

By the time I reached our street my feet had gone numb and my phone had died, so the decision about pressing the green circle was taken out of my hands, and I was almost grateful. The houses were dark, one after another, except ours. The kitchen light was on, yellow and ordinary, laid across the wet path like a doormat.

I stood at the gate for a long time. I thought about what I would say and every sentence sounded either like a defence or like a performance. In the end, when I let myself in, I did not say any of them. She was at the table with the untouched mug, her coat still on as if she had been about to go out and look for me and had not been able to decide which way.

"The last bus had gone," I said, and my voice cracked on the word gone.

She looked at me for a moment, and then she moved the second chair out from the table with her foot, quietly, the way you would for somebody you had been saving a place for. I sat. Neither of us said anything for a while, and it was the best conversation we had had in months.

task: Creative writing: write a short story or descriptive piece that begins with the line 'The last bus had already left.'
text:
The last bus had already left. Jake was very angry and also scared because it was dark and he was in a place he did not know. He looked at his watch and it was 11 o clock at night. He had been at his friend Tom's house playing video games and he had forgotten the time because they were having so much fun. Now he was stuck.

"Oh no," said Jake. "What am I going to do now?"

He decided to call his mum but his phone was dead. This was very bad. He was feeling very nervous so he decided to walk home. It was about five miles and he knew the way, or at least he thought he did. He started walking down the road and it was very quiet and cold. The moon was big and bright in the sky. There were trees everywhere and they looked scary in the dark.

Suddenly he heard a noise behind him. He turned around quickly but there was nothing there. His heart was beating really fast. He started to walk faster and faster. Then he heard it again, and this time it was closer. He started to run as fast as he could, and he ran past a big old house that looked haunted. There was a light on in one of the windows and he thought he saw somebody looking out.

Jake kept running until he could not run any more. He stopped to catch his breath next to a bench. He was sweating even though it was cold. Then he saw a shadow coming towards him from the trees. He was so scared that he could not move. It came closer and closer and then it jumped out and it was just a cat. Jake laughed because he felt silly. The cat looked at him and meowed and then it went away.

"It was only a cat," he said to himself. "I am so stupid."

He carried on walking and after a while he came to a crossroads and he did not know which way to go. There was a sign but it was broken and he could not read it. He thought left was the right way, but then he thought it was right. He was very confused. In the end he went left because it looked like the way he had come with his dad in the car one time.

He walked for a very long time. His feet were hurting and he was very tired and he wanted to be in bed. He thought about his mum and how worried she would be. She would probably be really angry with him but he did not care because he just wanted to go home. He also thought about how he should have left Tom's house earlier and he promised himself he would never do it again.

After what felt like hours he saw some lights in the distance. It was a petrol station. Jake was so happy that he ran towards it. Inside there was a man behind the counter who had a beard and looked quite friendly. Jake explained what had happened and the man said he could use the phone. Jake rang his mum and she answered straight away.

"Jake! Where are you? I have been so worried!" she said in a shaky voice.

"I am at the petrol station on Mill Road. I missed the bus and my phone died. I am really sorry mum," said Jake.

"Stay there, I am coming to get you right now," she said.

While he waited, the man gave him a hot chocolate for free and said that he should be more careful. Jake said thank you and drank it, and it was the best hot chocolate he had ever had. About ten minutes later his mum arrived in the car. She got out and hugged him really tightly and she was crying a bit. Jake felt really bad that he had made her upset.

On the way home she did not say much, but she said that she was glad he was safe. Jake said sorry again and promised he would never miss the last bus again. When they got home he went straight to bed and fell asleep as soon as his head touched the pillow.

The next day he woke up and he felt much better. He told Tom what happened and Tom said that it sounded really scary. Jake said it was but that he had learned a lesson. From that day on he always checked the time and always made sure his phone was charged. He never missed the last bus again and he was always home on time. The end.

task: Creative writing: write a short story or descriptive piece that begins with the line 'The last bus had already left.'
text: The last bus had already left and I was at the bus stop. I was very sad because I had no other way to get home and it was late. I was with my freind Ali and he was sad too. We went to town to go shopping and then we went to the cinema and we forgot the time. It was dark and it was cold and we was scared. Ali said lets walk home but I said it was to far. Then we saw a man he looked scary and he came to us. He said do you need help and we said no. He was a nice man in the end he was just being nice. He gave us a lift in his car and we went home. My mum was very angry she said where have you been I was worrying. I said sorry mum and she said go to bed. I went to bed and I was happy that I was at home. In the morning I told my sister about it and she laughed at me. She said you was so stupid for missing the bus. I said it was not my fault it was Ali fault because he wanted to go to the cinema. Then I went to school and I told everyone and they all laughed. After that I never missed the bus again and I learned that you should always look at the time. It was the worst day of my life and I will never forget it. The end

task: Write a persuasive speech to your school assembly arguing for or against banning single-use plastic from the school canteen.
text:
Good morning, teachers, and good morning, everyone.

Let me start with a number. Every day, our canteen hands out around four hundred plastic forks, cups and wrappers. By the time most of you have finished lunch, that plastic has been in your hand for about ten minutes. It will be on this planet for about four hundred years. Ten minutes of convenience against four centuries of waste: I do not think that is a fair trade, and I believe it is time for our school to ban single-use plastic from the canteen.

I know what some of you are thinking. "It is only a fork. What difference can one school make?" It is a fair question, and I want to answer it honestly. One fork does nothing. But we are not one fork. We are twelve hundred students, five days a week, thirty-eight weeks a year. If you do the sum, and I did, because I had to prove it to myself, that is over a hundred thousand pieces of plastic a year from this building alone. Small things, multiplied, are not small any more.

Some people will say that a ban is unfair, that it will make lunch more expensive or more difficult. But think about what we are really being asked to give up. A paper cup instead of a plastic one. A wooden fork instead of a plastic fork. A reusable bottle, which many of you already carry, instead of a bottle you will throw away within the hour. Is that really a sacrifice? Or is it just a habit we have never been asked to question?

And we should remember that this is not an idea invented by one angry student. Cities and countries are already doing it. Last year, our neighbours at the school across the river switched to compostable packaging, and their canteen manager told me that after the first two weeks, nobody noticed. Nobody. If they can do it, why should we be the school that decides we cannot?

There is also a bigger reason, and it is one I feel strongly about. We are the generation who will be living with the consequences of today's waste. Our parents may not see the oceans choked with plastic, but we might. We will be the ones explaining to our own children why the beaches are closed. Surely it is better to be the generation that said, "enough", than the one that said, "it was only a fork".

Of course, I am not asking you to take my word for it. I am asking the student council, and the teachers who sit on the canteen committee, to hear a simple proposal. A three-month trial. No plastic cutlery, no plastic cups, no plastic wrapping on food prepared in our own kitchen. At the end of the three months, we will measure how much we saved and how much we spent, and we will decide together. If I am wrong, the plastic can come back. If I am right, we will have shown that a school can lead, and not just follow.

So let me leave you with this. The next time you pick up a plastic fork, I want you to hold it up and look at it, really look at it. Ask yourself: where will this be when I am an old man, or an old woman? Then ask yourself whether you are happy for it to still be here, long after you have forgotten the sandwich it came with.

We can be the generation that changed this. We can start today, in this canteen, with this lunch. I am asking you to stand with me. Thank you.

task: Write an analytical essay on how F. Scott Fitzgerald presents the American Dream in The Great Gatsby.
text:
The Great Gatsby is a very famous novel written by F. Scott Fitzgerald in the 1920s. It is about a man called Jay Gatsby who is very rich and who has a lot of parties at his big mansion on Long Island. The story is told by a man called Nick Carraway who lives next door. In this essay I am going to write about the American Dream in the novel and how Fitzgerald shows it, and I am going to say what happens in the story as well so that I can explain it properly.

At the start of the novel Nick moves to New York to learn about the bond business. He rents a small house in West Egg, which is next to a big mansion that belongs to Gatsby. Nick goes to see his cousin Daisy and her husband Tom in East Egg. Tom is very rich and he is also very big and strong and he plays polo. Daisy is very pretty and she has a voice that sounds like money. They live in a big house with a lawn and Nick has dinner with them. At the dinner he meets Jordan Baker who is a golfer. Then they talk about lots of things and Tom gets a phone call from someone and it turns out he is having an affair. So this is the beginning of the novel and it shows that the people are rich but not very happy.

Then Nick goes to the valley of ashes which is a place between West Egg and New York. It is a very grey and dirty place and it is where the poor people live. There is a billboard with the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg on it and the eyes look over everything. Tom takes Nick to meet his mistress Myrtle Wilson who is married to George Wilson, who owns a garage. This shows that there are rich and poor people in the novel and that the American Dream is not the same for everyone. The poor people are in the valley of ashes and the rich people are in East Egg and West Egg. So Fitzgerald is showing that the American Dream is not very good for some people.

After that Nick goes to one of Gatsby's parties. The party is very big and there is lots of music and lots of drinking and people are dancing and having fun. There are lots of people at the party that nobody knows and some of them have not even been invited. Nick meets Gatsby at the party and he is very nice and he has a really nice smile. Gatsby then tells him he went to Oxford and that he is from a rich family, but this turns out to be lies. Later we find out that Gatsby was really called James Gatz and he was from a poor family in North Dakota. He changed his name and he got rich by doing illegal things with Meyer Wolfsheim. So the American Dream is that you can come from nothing and become rich, which is what Gatsby did, and this is what Fitzgerald is showing us.

Gatsby then asks Nick to arrange a meeting with Daisy because he loves her. They had been together before he went to the war but she married Tom while he was away. So Nick has a tea party at his house and Gatsby comes and he is very nervous and he knocks over a clock. Then Daisy and Gatsby start meeting each other and Gatsby shows Daisy his house and all his shirts and Daisy cries. This shows that Gatsby wants Daisy because he has lots of money now and he wants to be with her. Gatsby's dream is really to be with Daisy and this is also part of the American Dream because he thinks that if he has money he can have anything, including Daisy.

Then there is a scene at the Plaza Hotel where everyone goes to New York in the heat and Tom and Gatsby have an argument. Tom says that Gatsby is a criminal and that Daisy will never leave him. Gatsby says that Daisy never loved Tom, but Daisy is not sure. Then they drive back and Daisy is driving the yellow car and she hits Myrtle and kills her but Gatsby takes the blame. This is a very bad part of the story and it shows how careless the rich people are. So the American Dream is a bit bad here because the rich people do not care about the poor people.

After this George Wilson thinks that Gatsby was the one who killed Myrtle, because the car was his, and he goes to Gatsby's house and shoots him in the pool and then shoots himself. This is the end of Gatsby and it is very sad. Hardly anyone comes to his funeral except Nick and Gatsby's father, and the people who came to his parties do not come. Nick thinks that they are a rotten crowd and that Gatsby is worth the whole damn bunch put together. Then Nick goes back to the Midwest because he is tired of the East. So this is the end and it shows that the American Dream did not work for Gatsby.

Overall the American Dream in the novel is shown in lots of ways. It is shown through Gatsby who was poor and became rich. It is shown through the parties which were very big and fancy. It is shown through the valley of ashes where the poor people lived. It is also shown through Daisy and Tom who were rich and did not care about other people. I think that Fitzgerald is trying to say that the American Dream is not always good and that it can be bad for some people. Gatsby had the dream and he got a lot of money but he did not get Daisy and in the end he died.

In conclusion, Fitzgerald shows the American Dream in lots of different ways in the novel. The story of Gatsby is a very sad one and it shows that money does not make you happy. I think that it is a really good novel and it has a lot of things that you can learn from it. The American Dream is a big part of the novel and Fitzgerald shows it by what happens to Gatsby and the other characters. This is how Fitzgerald shows the American Dream in The Great Gatsby and why it is important in the novel.

task: Write an analytical essay on how the writer presents character in a text of your choice, or (if choosing the creative option) a short story about a character facing a difficult decision.
text:
Nobody in our building called it the lift. It was the box, and on the fourth floor of Marsden Court the box had been broken for eleven weeks, which meant that Mrs Okafor, who was eighty-one and lived on the seventh, had not left her flat since the second week of September.

I knew this because I lived directly below her and because, every Thursday, I heard her tapping on the floor with the end of her walking stick: three taps, a pause, one tap. I had been told what it meant by my dad. It meant I'm alright, don't worry. It also meant, though nobody said it, that someone should come and see.

On the Thursday I am telling you about, there was no tapping. I stood in my bedroom with my history homework open on the desk and listened to the ceiling for almost ten minutes. Nothing. A pipe knocked somewhere. A television laughed through a wall. I told myself she was asleep.

The decision I had to make was a small one, and that is what made it so hard. I could knock on her door, and risk finding something I did not want to find. Or I could carry on with my homework, tell my dad when he got back at six, and let an adult handle it. Everyone, I knew, would say that the second option was sensible. My stomach said it was the coward's option.

I went up the stairs. Seven flights is not many, but in that building the stairwell smells of damp and old chip fat, and every landing has a window that does not open, so that the air gets thicker as you climb. By the fifth floor my legs were burning. By the sixth I had begun to bargain with myself. Just to the door, I said. Just listen at the door.

Her door was painted a faded green, and the brass number seven had slipped so that it hung at an angle, as if tired. I knocked once. Then, because nobody answered, I knocked again, harder, and said, in a voice that did not sound like mine, "Mrs Okafor? It is Daniel from downstairs."

For a long moment there was only the hum of the corridor light. Then, from somewhere deep inside the flat, a thin voice said, "I cannot get up. The door is not locked."

I have thought about that sentence many times since. The door was not locked. She had left it unlocked for eleven weeks, in case.

Inside, the flat was warm and smelled of boiled rice and lavender. She was sitting in her armchair with a blanket over her knees, and her stick lay on the carpet where it had slipped out of her hand. She had been trying to reach it for two hours, she told me, and she was too proud to shout. When I picked it up and put it into her hands, she held on to my wrist for longer than she needed to, and I felt how light her fingers were, like paper that had been folded and unfolded too often.

"You are a good boy," she said.

"I only came up the stairs," I said, and felt embarrassed, because it sounded like a joke and it was not.

I made her a cup of tea in a kitchen so tidy it hurt to look at. While the kettle boiled, I saw the calendar on the wall above the cooker. Every Thursday had a small cross drawn in pencil, and under each cross, in handwriting that grew shakier as the weeks went on, were two words: still here.

When my dad got home that evening, I told him everything, and he went very quiet, and then he said he would ring the council about the lift again, and this time he would not stop ringing. I did not say that it was not really about the lift. I did not say that it was about the three taps and the one, and how easy it is to hear a signal for eleven weeks without once climbing the stairs.

The next Thursday, at four o'clock, I stood in my room and waited. Three taps. A pause. One tap. I picked up my stick, which was the old curtain pole I had found in the cupboard, and I tapped back, once, to say that I had heard her. Then I went upstairs anyway.

task: Write an analytical essay on how Percy Bysshe Shelley presents the transience of power in the sonnet 'Ozymandias'.
text:
In "Ozymandias", Percy Bysshe Shelley presents political power as a fragile and ultimately self-defeating illusion. The sonnet turns on a bitter irony: a king who intended his monument to terrify future generations has left behind only a broken statue in an empty desert, and the very words he chose to express his greatness now announce his insignificance. Through its framing narrative, its fragmented imagery and the subversion of its own form, the poem argues that tyranny destroys itself, while the art that outlasts it belongs not to the ruler but to the sculptor.

Shelley first distances the reader from the king by using a layered narrative. The speaker does not claim to have seen the statue; he reports the words of "a traveller from an antique land". This double remove, a story within a story, has two effects. It lends the poem the weight of rumour passed down through time, so that Ozymandias is already half-legend, and it makes the reader participate in the process of forgetting that the poem describes. By the time the ruin reaches us it has been retold, interpreted and softened. The adjective "antique" is carefully chosen: it can mean ancient, but it also suggests something collectable, a curiosity for the museum, which reduces an empire to an object to be stared at.

The description of the statue gradually dismantles the king's body. We are shown "two vast and trunkless legs of stone" standing alone, and then, half-sunk, "a shattered visage", the face lying in the sand. The word "trunkless" is crucial. Without the torso, the arms and the head, the legs have lost the capacity to act, to hold a sceptre or to command; the body of the state has been literally dismembered. The "shattered visage" is equally telling, since the face is where authority is read. Yet Shelley does not let the face lose its personality: the "frown, / And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command" survive. The sculptor, he writes, "well those passions read", which are "stamped on these lifeless things". Here the poem makes a quiet, double-edged compliment. The passions of the tyrant have outlasted his reign, but they have done so only because an artist captured them. The line that follows, "The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed", is syntactically ambiguous, because "mocked" can mean both ridiculed and imitated. The sculptor's hand mocked the king's passions by copying them, and so the artist both preserves and subtly undermines the man who paid him.

The inscription at the centre of the poem is where the irony becomes explicit. The pedestal reads: "My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; / Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!" The capitalisation of "Works" and "Mighty" and the imperative verb "Look" capture the king's grandiloquence, and the exclamation mark seems to project his voice across the page. But the reader sees what the king could not. The "Mighty" are meant to despair at his achievements, yet we, who have been shown the ruin, are invited to despair for a different reason, that all human achievement is as perishable as his. The first line of the inscription is also telling. A king who must announce his own name suggests that he feared it might be forgotten, and the title "King of Kings" is hollow without any subjects left to be ruled.

Shelley's final lines complete the reversal with a strikingly empty landscape: "Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away." The blunt statement "Nothing beside remains" is a caesura-heavy half-line that stops the sentence dead, imitating the way the empire stopped. The adjective "colossal" is in tension with the noun "Wreck", so that the sheer size of the king's ambitions seems to make his fall more complete. The sibilance and the long vowels of "lone and level sands" slow the rhythm and spread the line out across the page, enacting the vastness of the desert that has consumed him. The word "level" has a subtle political resonance too: the sands erase all hierarchy, and the king has at last been made equal to everyone else.

Even the form of the poem plays its part. A sonnet is traditionally a controlled, ordered form, associated with love and with praise, and Shelley disrupts it. The rhyme scheme refuses to settle into either the Petrarchan or the Shakespearean pattern, so that the poem, like the statue, seems to have been assembled from fragments. This formal instability reflects the poem's political message. If Ozymandias represents rigid, absolute authority, then Shelley's irregular sonnet, with its enjambment and shifting rhythm, quietly enacts the freedom and the change that such authority fears.

It is worth remembering that Shelley, a radical who disapproved of monarchy, wrote this poem in 1817, when the rulers of Europe were attempting to restore their thrones after the fall of Napoleon. In that context the poem reads not just as a reflection on the ancient past but as a warning to his own contemporaries. The "sneer of cold command" does not belong only to an Egyptian pharaoh.

In conclusion, "Ozymandias" is a poem about the failure of power to secure its own memory. Shelley strips the king of his body, his audience and his empire, leaving only a pronouncement that mocks its speaker. And yet the poem suggests that something does survive: the sculptor's skill, and the poet's, which is capable of turning a tyrant's vanity into a lesson for those who come after.
